title: Why causal stories are tempting
passage: People prefer coherent explanations even when evidence is incomplete. The most obvious explanation is rarely the only one available. Good reasoning therefore requires more than collecting facts. It requires deciding which facts matter, how strongly they support a claim, and what alternative explanations remain possible. A strong account does not eliminate uncertainty; it makes uncertainty visible and proportionate to the evidence. In this case, the key is to ask what the claim leaves out as well as what it explains. The broader lesson is that precision is not the same as complexity. Often the clearest sentence is the one that has already done the most thinking.

title: What makes an idea travel
passage: Ideas spread when they are memorable, adaptable, and socially useful. A useful way to think about this is to separate visible outcomes from the processes that produce them. Institutions, habits, incentives, and timing often interact in ways that are difficult to observe directly. What appears to be a single decision may actually be the cumulative result of many smaller choices. This is why careful analysis pays attention not only to outcomes, but also to sequence, context, and who had the authority to act. In this case, the key is to ask what the claim leaves out as well as what it explains. For a careful writer, the goal is not to make the issue sound more complicated than it is. The goal is to describe the complication precisely enough that a reader can see why it matters.
